questions.q: What specific problem shows up once the same app runs in dev, staging, and prod with hand-written Kubernetes manifests?
options: Kubernetes refuses to schedule Pods unless every environment uses identical YAML
kubectl apply requires a paid license for more than one environment
Pods automatically sync their configuration across environments, which is unsafe
Near-identical Deployment files have to be edited correctly in multiple places, or environments silently drift apart
questions.explain: Maintaining three nearly-identical manifests means every real change — image tag, env var, resource limit — must be made correctly in each file, or dev/staging/prod drift out of sync.

options: A package manager for Kubernetes that installs applications packaged as versioned charts
A replacement for kubectl that bypasses the Kubernetes API
A container runtime that replaces containerd
A monitoring dashboard built into the Kubernetes control plane
questions.explain: Helm is a package manager: it resolves a chart against a set of values and generates the plain Kubernetes YAML that still gets applied through the Kubernetes API.

questions.q: In a Helm template like `image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"`, what does the `{{ }}` placeholder get replaced with?
options: A random value generated by the Kubernetes API server
Whatever value is supplied for that key at install or upgrade time, typically from values.yaml
The name of the chart itself
Nothing — it is only a comment and has no effect on the rendered manifest
questions.explain: Templates reference placeholders; Helm fills them in from the values supplied at install/upgrade time, which is what lets one template serve every environment.

questions.q: Which prior-course concept does Helm's template-plus-values split most directly parallel?
options: Docker multi-stage builds separating build tools from the runtime image
Kubernetes ConfigMaps mounted as environment variables
Terraform's single resource definition paired with separate per-environment variable files
A container registry's image tagging scheme
questions.explain: Just as Terraform keeps one resource definition and supplies different values per environment through variable files, Helm keeps one chart template and supplies different values per environment through values files.

questions.q: Does Helm replace kubectl's role in talking to a cluster?
options: No — Helm still generates plain Kubernetes YAML and applies it through the Kubernetes API; it adds templating, values, and release history on top
Yes — once Helm is installed, kubectl can no longer be used on that cluster
Yes — Helm uses a completely separate API that bypasses the Kubernetes control plane
No — Helm only works for retrieving logs, never for deploying anything
questions.explain: Helm doesn't bypass Kubernetes; it renders templates into ordinary manifests and applies them through the same Kubernetes API kubectl uses, while adding templating and release tracking.
